title: Just Align 𝒙: Aligning Predictions, Not Representations

paper.title: Just Align 𝒙 \bm{x} : Aligning Predictions, Not Representations
paper.abstract: Abstract Representation alignment has become an effective way to accelerate diffusion training, but its benefits do not transfer reliably to pixel-space clean-image prediction. In JiT, we find that auxiliary feature alignment can improve access to semantic features while reducing access to image variation needed for clean-image prediction, creating a mismatch between the auxiliary objective and the denoising task. This suggests a different principle: auxiliary supervision should improve the prediction target itself rather than impose a separate representation target . We introduce JA x \bm{x} (Just Align 𝒙 \bm{x} ), a prediction-supervision method that aligns clean-image predictions across noise levels. JA x \bm{x} couples a noisier student observation with a cleaner observation through a Markov degradation that preserves the original JiT input distribution. Under this coupling, the oracle prediction from the cleaner state has the same conditional mean as the optimal JiT target, while its conditional target covariance is no greater. Thus, oracle prediction alignment preserves the population JiT objective up to a constant while providing a lower-variance training target. To make this construction practical with an imperfect EMA teacher, JA x \bm{x} combines ground-truth supervision with a reliability-gated coupling band that selects nearby teacher states based on prediction risk. On ImageNet 256×256, JA x \bm{x} consistently improves FID and accelerates convergence across JiT-B/16, L/16, and H/16, without an external encoder or changes to the architecture or sampling procedure. Gradient diagnostics further show reduced minibatch gradient variance, while ablations demonstrate that the gains cannot be explained by time reweighting alone. These results show that prediction-space supervision provides a simple and principled alternative to representation alignment for pixel-space generative models.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion and flow-based models have emerged as dominant paradigms for visual generation, transforming noise into data through iterative denoising ( Ho et al., 2020 ) or continuous transport ( Song et al., 2021 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) . Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) provide a scalable architecture for modeling these generative dynamics ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) . Beyond architectural scaling, recent studies ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Singh et al., 2026a ; Jiang et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Chefer et al., 2026 ; Wang and He, 2025 ) have shown that aligning or regularizing internal representations can substantially accelerate DiT training. However, most of this progress has been developed in latent diffusion ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) , where an autoencoder compresses images before generative modeling. This introduces a reconstruction–generation trade-off: latent representations must preserve image details while remaining suitable for generation ( Leng et al., 2025 ; Yao et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ; Singh et al., 2026b ) . Pixel-space generation removes this intermediate representation but requires the model to directly predict high-dimensional images. Motivated by the low-dimensional manifold structure of natural images, JiT ( Li and He, 2026 ) addresses this challenge through clean-image prediction with large pixel patches, providing a simple and effective framework without pretrained tokenizers or auxiliary representation objectives. This difference in prediction space raises a fundamental question: what auxiliary supervision is appropriate for pixel-space 𝐱 \bm{x} -prediction? A direct transfer of representation alignment is not always effective. PixelREPA ( Shin et al., 2026 ) shows that applying REPA can accelerate early learning but may degrade generation quality later in training, motivating adaptations to the mismatch between semantic features and pixel-level reconstruction. In the JiT settings we evaluate, transferred hidden self-alignment and regularization methods provide limited gains, while the advantage of REPA in low-resolution image generation can also reverse as model size decreases. One important difference is the input dimensionality: DiT-B/2 maps a 16 16 -dimensional latent patch to a 768 768 -dimensional hidden token, whereas JiT-B/16 maps 768 768 pixel values to the same hidden width. Although these dimensions alone do not determine model capacity, they highlight a potential conflict between auxiliary feature learning and clean-image prediction. Our probes show increased linear accessibility of aligned semantic features together with reduced accessibility of clean-image variation not linearly explained by those features (Section 3 ). These observations motivate a different principle: rather than imposing an auxiliary representation target, auxiliary supervision should directly support the prediction target of the generative objective. We therefore ask whether an auxiliary prediction target can preserve the conditional mean required by JiT while reducing the conditional target variance. Based on this principle, we introduce JA x \bm{x} (Just Align 𝒙 \bm{x} ), which aligns clean-image predictions across noise levels. Specifically, we couple a cleaner observation with the student’s noisier input through a Markov degradation that preserves the original student-input marginal. Under this coupling, the optimal clean-image predictions satisfy a martingale consistency property: averaging the cleaner prediction conditioned on the noisier observation recovers the optimal prediction at that noise level. With the original JiT time distribution and loss weighting, this oracle supervision induces the same population regression objective up to a parameter-independent constant, while its conditional target covariance is no greater than that of direct clean-image supervision. In practice, JA x \bm{x} uses an exponential-moving-average (EMA) teacher to predict 𝒙 \bm{x} from the cleaner observation. Because teacher errors can bias the auxiliary target, we retain supervision from the ground-truth clean image and introduce a reliability-gated coupling band that selects nearby teacher states according to an empirical prediction-risk criterion. This selection balances the potential variance reduction from cleaner targets against the error introduced by the evolving teacher. JA x \bm{x} requires no external encoder and leaves the JiT architecture and sampling procedure unchanged. Across model scales, it improves generation quality and accelerates convergence in training epochs. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We empirically examine the limitations of hidden representation alignment in JiT and identify conditional target consistency as a guiding principle for auxiliary prediction supervision. • We introduce Markov-coupled prediction supervision and establish conditional-mean consistency, population loss equivalence, and conditional covariance reduction for oracle predictions. • We develop reliability-gated pair selection for an evolving EMA teacher and demonstrate improved generation quality and faster convergence across JiT model scales.

sections.heading: Pixel-space diffusion
sections.text: Early diffusion models directly learn the generative process in RGB space ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) , whereas modern large-scale systems commonly adopt latent diffusion to reduce the spatial and computational burden through a pretrained autoencoder ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) . This efficiency, however, makes generation dependent on a separately learned latent space and its reconstruction properties. Recent works ( Baade et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2025b ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Yu et al., 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026 ; Li and He, 2026 ) revisit end-to-end pixel-space generation from several directions: PixelFlow progressively increases spatial resolution along the generative trajectory ( Chen et al., 2025b ) ; PixelDiT and DeCo separate semantic or low-frequency modeling from pixel-level details ( Yu et al., 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) ; JiT instead studies a particularly minimal formulation based on large pixel patches and direct clean-image prediction, showing that high-dimensional RGB observations can be modeled without a tokenizer or an auxiliary decoder ( Li and He, 2026 ) . Our work retains this minimal JiT architecture and focuses on accelerating its optimization without introducing a separate representation space or modifying its sampling process.

sections.heading: Representation Learning.
sections.text: Beyond serving as a compressed generation space ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) , learned representations can provide useful structure and supervision for generative modeling. Semantic tokenizers and representation autoencoders explore generation spaces that combine semantic information with image reconstruction ( Chen et al., 2025a ; Zheng et al., 2026 ; Singh et al., 2026b ) , while representation alignment methods use learned features to guide the optimization of generative models. REPA ( Yu et al., 2025 ) aligns intermediate diffusion features with representations from pretrained visual encoders, improving the hidden representation leading to better generation quality and training efficiency in latent DiTs. Subsequent work explores the choice of alignment targets ( Singh et al., 2026a ) , the placement and duration of supervision ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , and the joint adaptation of the tokenizer and denoising network ( Leng et al., 2025 ) . Self-alignment methods ( Jiang et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Chefer et al., 2026 ) further investigate whether useful representation guidance can be obtained from the generative model itself, reducing reliance on external encoders. However, changing the source of supervision does not necessarily remove the additional representational demands imposed by hidden-feature alignment. PixelREPA adapts feature alignment to pixel-space clean-image prediction ( Shin et al., 2026 ) . Nevertheless, it retains hidden representations as the alignment target, potentially imposing demands that compete with pixel reconstruction within shared model capacity. This motivates aligning clean-image predictions themselves: our method provides additional supervision for the denoising task without requiring hidden features to match a separate representation target, with conditional consistency and variance reduction established under a Markov coupling for optimal predictions.

sections.heading: Training behavior.
sections.text: Figure 1: REPA initially improves FID on JiT-S/4 at ImageNet 32 × 32 32\times 32 , but the advantage reverses later in training. PixelREPA ( Shin et al., 2026 ) relates the difficulty of applying REPA in pixel space to the mismatch between high-resolution pixels and compressed semantic features, reporting improvements at ImageNet 32 × 32 32\times 32 but later degradation at 256 × 256 256\times 256 . We revisit the low-resolution regime with a smaller JiT-S/4 (Fig. 1 ). REPA improves FID from 16.37 16.37 to 16.08 16.08 at 50 epochs and from 12.89 12.89 to 12.03 12.03 at 100 epochs. At 200 and 400 epochs, however, it obtains FIDs of 10.79 10.79 and 9.90 9.90 , compared with 9.15 9.15 and 7.65 7.65 for vanilla JiT. Thus, reducing resolution does not by itself ensure sustained gains from feature alignment. Our JiT-B/16 comparisons also show limited gains from directly transferred hidden self-alignment and regularization methods (Table 1 ). These observations motivate examining the interaction between auxiliary feature learning and clean-image prediction in the tested JiT settings.

They provide an empirical motivation to study auxiliary supervision whose relation to the denoising target can be analyzed directly.

sections.heading: 3.2 What Should an Auxiliary Prediction Target Preserve?
sections.text: These observations motivate auxiliary supervision directly on the clean-image prediction. To keep this supervision aligned with JiT’s denoising task, a target Y Y with finite second moments should satisfy conditional target consistency : 𝔼 ⁡ [ Y ∣ U t ] = 𝔼 ⁡ [ X ∣ U t ] = m t ​ ( Z t , c ) . \mathbb{E}[Y\mid U_{t}]=\mathbb{E}[X\mid U_{t}]=m_{t}(Z_{t},c). (3) This condition preserves the population regression target required by JiT. Consistency alone, however, does not explain how an auxiliary target can improve training: the clean-image target X X already satisfies this condition. A potential benefit lies in reducing the variability of the supervision. Conditional on a noisy input U t U_{t} , clean-image targets vary around the posterior mean; under squared regression, this target variation contributes to stochastic-gradient variability. We therefore seek a target that retains the same conditional mean while reducing conditional target variance, expressed by the covariance ordering Cov ⁡ ( Y ∣ U t ) ⪯ Cov ⁡ ( X ∣ U t ) , \operatorname{Cov}(Y\mid U_{t})\preceq\operatorname{Cov}(X\mid U_{t}), (4) where ⪯ \preceq denotes the positive-semidefinite order. This provides a possible optimization benefit while preserving the underlying regression task. In Section 4 , we construct a target from a cleaner, Markov-coupled observation and establish both properties for oracle clean-image predictions. We then address the approximation error of an actual EMA teacher through ground-truth supervision and reliability-gated pair selection.

sections.heading: 4 Method
sections.text: We present JA x \bm{x} , which supervises clean-image predictions across Markov-coupled noise levels. sections.heading: Experimental setup.
sections.text: We evaluate on ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 using the JiT-B/16, L/16, and H/16 architectures and base training recipe ( Li and He, 2026 ) , with a shared alignment weight λ = 0.5 \lambda=0.5 . We report FID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) and Inception Score (IS) ( Salimans et al., 2016 ) using 50K generated samples. Sampling follows JiT with a 50-step Heun ODE solver and CFG ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) over the interval [ 0.1 , 1 ] [0.1,1] ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ) . Full training, EMA, and evaluation settings are provided in Appendix C .

sections.heading: Generation quality and convergence.

sections.heading: Comparison with feature alignment methods.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented JA x \bm{x} , a prediction-supervision method for JiT motivated by the observed limitations of hidden representation alignment. Under Markov coupling, oracle clean-image predictions preserve the required conditional mean and reduce conditional target covariance, with a population loss equivalent to JiT’s up to a constant. The practical method combines an EMA teacher with direct clean-image supervision and reliability-gated pair selection to address teacher approximation error. Experiments demonstrate improved final FID and faster convergence in training epochs across JiT scales, without external encoders or changes to the architecture and sampling procedure. Ablations show that time reweighting alone and fixed-gap alignment after warmup do not reproduce these gains, supporting the contributions of both teacher targets and reliability-gated selection. Gradient diagnostics further show lower normalized gradient variance and mean-squared deviation from the JiT population gradient. Combining JA x \bm{x} with PixelREPA also improves FID in the evaluated JiT-B/16 setting.

sections.heading: Comparison with representation-based supervision.
sections.text: Figure 7 compares JA x \bm{x} with four representative strategies for augmenting generative training. Auxiliary representation learning introduces self-supervised tasks, such as masked reconstruction, while external representation alignment uses a pretrained encoder to supervise hidden features. SRA replaces the external encoder with an EMA teacher and aligns shallow student features with deeper teacher features. Self-Flow further introduces dual-timestep scheduling, using mixed-noise student inputs and uniformly cleaner teacher inputs for feature alignment. JA x \bm{x} instead applies alignment directly to clean predictions, using reliability-gated Markov coupling to construct teacher–student pairs. This formulation requires neither an external representation encoder nor an additional trainable alignment head, and avoids imposing an auxiliary matching constraint on hidden representations. Since prediction alignment and representation alignment act at different levels, they are complementary and can be combined.

sections.heading: Stochastic and trajectory consistency.
sections.text: Consistent Diffusion Models ( Daras et al., 2023 ) enforce a martingale property under the model’s learned reverse process to mitigate sampling drift. JA x \bm{x} constructs teacher–student observations directly through an explicit forward Markov coupling X → Z s → Z t X\to Z_{s}\to Z_{t} , preserving the JiT corruption marginals without simulating model-generated trajectories. This coupling makes the cleaner oracle prediction a valid regression target for the noisier student: its conditional expectation equals the student’s desired posterior mean. The resulting oracle alignment objective therefore has the same population gradient as JiT, with reduced conditional target covariance. Consistency Models ( Song et al., 2023 ) instead learn a common endpoint prediction along each probability-flow ODE trajectory for one- or few-step generation. Our stochastic coupling permits oracle predictions to differ across individual pairs while preserving their conditional expectation. This distinction enables auxiliary prediction supervision within the existing JiT training and sampling framework.

sections.heading: Low-variance prediction targets.
sections.text: Stable Velocity ( Yang et al., 2026 ) introduces StableVM, which reduces target variance through a weighted aggregation of conditional velocities over multiple reference data points. JA x \bm{x} obtains its oracle target by posterior conditioning on a coupled, cleaner observation of the same image. The Markov construction jointly establishes conditional-mean correctness and identifies the exact covariance removed: the expected posterior uncertainty remaining at the teacher observation. Both properties matter, since a low-variance target can still supervise the wrong conditional mean, as illustrated by the Gaussian example in Appendix A.3 . The analysis also informs teacher-time selection: closer oracle targets provide greater variance reduction, whereas practical EMA targets must be sufficiently reliable. Our reliability-gated coupling band operationalizes this trade-off using an empirical reliability frontier and bounded log-SNR separation, retaining JiT-only supervision when no feasible pair exists. The contribution thus connects an explicit coupling, a posterior-based target construction, and reliability-aware pair selection into a practical prediction-alignment method.

sections.heading: Appendix D Limitation and Future Work
sections.text: Our evaluation focuses on class-conditional image generation, leaving large-scale text-to-image and video generation unexplored. We expect JA x \bm{x} to be effective in these settings as well, since its prediction alignment mechanism does not rely on an external pretrained representation encoder. This property may be particularly valuable for video generation, where higher-dimensional spatiotemporal representations can intensify competition for model capacity between representation alignment and denoising. By aligning clean predictions directly, JA x \bm{x} avoids introducing an additional hidden-representation matching objective. Moreover, JA x \bm{x} is complementary to hidden-representation alignment methods and can be used together with them, offering a promising direction for future work. Our reliability frontier and several hyperparameter choices are empirically determined. In the future, we plan to systematically study how to better translate the benefits of oracle targets to practical EMA teachers and develop more principled strategies for hyperparameter selection. sections.text: The additional training workload consists of stop-gradient teacher evaluation on active samples, elementwise EMA updates, and periodic risk calibration. The teacher workload scales with the active fraction, while full-batch normalization keeps the loss weight of each active target fixed. The student architecture and sampling procedure remain unchanged, so JA x \bm{x} introduces no additional inference cost. For an approximate compute accounting, let F F denote the cost of a full-batch student forward pass and count a backward pass as two forward passes. The resulting estimated multiplier is approximately 1.22 × 1.22\times in the saturated regime and 1.21 × 1.21\times averaged over the full training run, during which the active fraction is initially lower. Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.00600v1 [cs.CV] 30 Sep 2026 Just Align 𝒙 \bm{x} : Aligning Predictions, Not Representations Yuyao Zhang Yuwei Hu Ziyang Mai Yu-Wing Tai Affiliation: Dartmouth College Abstract Representation alignment has become an effective way to accelerate diffusion training, but its benefits do not transfer reliably to pixel-space clean-image prediction. In JiT, we find that auxiliary feature alignment can improve access to semantic features while reducing access to image variation needed for clean-image prediction, creating a mismatch between the auxiliary objective and the denoising task. This suggests a different principle: auxiliary supervision should improve the prediction target itself rather than impose a separate representation target . We introduce JA x \bm{x} (Just Align 𝒙 \bm{x} ), a prediction-supervision method that aligns clean-image predictions across noise levels. JA x \bm{x} couples a noisier student observation with a cleaner observation through a Markov degradation that preserves the original JiT input distribution. Under this coupling, the oracle prediction from the cleaner state has the same conditional mean as the optimal JiT target, while its conditional target covariance is no greater. Thus, oracle prediction alignment preserves the population JiT objective up to a constant while providing a lower-variance training target. To make this construction practical with an imperfect EMA teacher, JA x \bm{x} combines ground-truth supervision with a reliability-gated coupling band that selects nearby teacher states based on prediction risk. On ImageNet 256×256, JA x \bm{x} consistently improves FID and accelerates convergence across JiT-B/16, L/16, and H/16, without an external encoder or changes to the architecture or sampling procedure. Gradient diagnostics further show reduced minibatch gradient variance, while ablations demonstrate that the gains cannot be explained by time reweighting alone. These results show that prediction-space supervision provides a simple and principled alternative to representation alignment for pixel-space generative models. 1 Introduction Diffusion and flow-based models have emerged as dominant paradigms for visual generation, transforming noise into data through iterative denoising ( Ho et al., 2020 ) or continuous transport ( Song et al., 2021 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) . Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) provide a scalable architecture for modeling these generative dynamics ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) . Beyond architectural scaling, recent studies ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Singh et al., 2026a ; Jiang et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Chefer et al., 2026 ; Wang and He, 2025 ) have shown that aligning or regularizing internal representations can substantially accelerate DiT training. However, most of this progress has been developed in latent diffusion ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) , where an autoencoder compresses images before generative modeling. This introduces a reconstruction–generation trade-off: latent representations must preserve image details while remaining suitable for generation ( Leng et al., 2025 ; Yao et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ; Singh et al., 2026b ) . Pixel-space generation removes this intermediate representation but requires the model to directly predict high-dimensional images. Motivated by the low-dimensional manifold structure of natural images, JiT ( Li and He, 2026 ) addresses this challenge through clean-image prediction with large pixel patches, providing a simple and effective framework without pretrained tokenizers or auxiliary representation objectives. This difference in prediction space raises a fundamental question: what auxiliary supervision is appropriate for pixel-space 𝐱 \bm{x} -prediction? A direct transfer of representation alignment is not always effective. PixelREPA ( Shin et al., 2026 ) shows that applying REPA can accelerate early learning but may degrade generation quality later in training, motivating adaptations to the mismatch between semantic features and pixel-level reconstruction. In the JiT settings we evaluate, transferred hidden self-alignment and regularization methods provide limited gains, while the advantage of REPA in low-resolution image generation can also reverse as model size decreases. One important difference is the input dimensionality: DiT-B/2 maps a 16 16 -dimensional latent patch to a 768 768 -dimensional hidden token, whereas JiT-B/16 maps 768 768 pixel values to the same hidden width. Although these dimensions alone do not determine model capacity, they highlight a potential conflict between auxiliary feature learning and clean-image prediction. Our probes show increased linear accessibility of aligned semantic features together with reduced accessibility of clean-image variation not linearly explained by those features (Section 3 ). These observations motivate a different principle: rather than imposing an auxiliary representation target, auxiliary supervision should directly support the prediction target of the generative objective. We therefore ask whether an auxiliary prediction target can preserve the conditional mean required by JiT while reducing the conditional target variance. Based on this principle, we introduce JA x \bm{x} (Just Align 𝒙 \bm{x} ), which aligns clean-image predictions across noise levels. Specifically, we couple a cleaner observation with the student’s noisier input through a Markov degradation that preserves the original student-input marginal. Under this coupling, the optimal clean-image predictions satisfy a martingale consistency property: averaging the cleaner prediction conditioned on the noisier observation recovers the optimal prediction at that noise level. With the original JiT time distribution and loss weighting, this oracle supervision induces the same population regression objective up to a parameter-independent constant, while its conditional target covariance is no greater than that of direct clean-image supervision. In practice, JA x \bm{x} uses an exponential-moving-average (EMA) teacher to predict 𝒙 \bm{x} from the cleaner observation. Because teacher errors can bias the auxiliary target, we retain supervision from the ground-truth clean image and introduce a reliability-gated coupling band that selects nearby teacher states according to an empirical prediction-risk criterion. This selection balances the potential variance reduction from cleaner targets against the error introduced by the evolving teacher. JA x \bm{x} requires no external encoder and leaves the JiT architecture and sampling procedure unchanged. Across model scales, it improves generation quality and accelerates convergence in training epochs. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We empirically examine the limitations of hidden representation alignment in JiT and identify conditional target consistency as a guiding principle for auxiliary prediction supervision. • We introduce Markov-coupled prediction supervision and establish conditional-mean consistency, population loss equivalence, and conditional covariance reduction for oracle predictions. • We develop reliability-gated pair selection for an evolving EMA teacher and demonstrate improved generation quality and faster convergence across JiT model scales. 2 Related Works Pixel-space diffusion Early diffusion models directly learn the generative process in RGB space ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) , whereas modern large-scale systems commonly adopt latent diffusion to reduce the spatial and computational burden through a pretrained autoencoder ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) . This efficiency, however, makes generation dependent on a separately learned latent space and its reconstruction properties. Recent works ( Baade et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2025b ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Yu et al., 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026 ; Li and He, 2026 ) revisit end-to-end pixel-space generation from several directions: PixelFlow progressively increases spatial resolution along the generative trajectory ( Chen et al., 2025b ) ; PixelDiT and DeCo separate semantic or low-frequency modeling from pixel-level details ( Yu et al., 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) ; JiT instead studies a particularly minimal formulation based on large pixel patches and direct clean-image prediction, showing that high-dimensional RGB observations can be modeled without a tokenizer or an auxiliary decoder ( Li and He, 2026 ) . Our work retains this minimal JiT architecture and focuses on accelerating its optimization without introducing a separate representation space or modifying its sampling process. Representation Learning. Beyond serving as a compressed generation space ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) , learned representations can provide useful structure and supervision for generative modeling. Semantic tokenizers and representation autoencoders explore generation spaces that combine semantic information with image reconstruction ( Chen et al., 2025a ; Zheng et al., 2026 ; Singh et al., 2026b ) , while representation alignment methods use learned features to guide the optimization of generative models. REPA ( Yu et al., 2025 ) aligns intermediate diffusion features with representations from pretrained visual encoders, improving the hidden representation leading to better generation quality and training efficiency in latent DiTs. Subsequent work explores the choice of alignment targets ( Singh et al., 2026a ) , the placement and duration of supervision ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , and the joint adaptation of the tokenizer and denoising network ( Leng et al., 2025 ) . Self-alignment methods ( Jiang et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Chefer et al., 2026 ) further investigate whether useful representation guidance can be obtained from the generative model itself, reducing reliance on external encoders. However, changing the source of supervision does not necessarily remove the additional representational demands imposed by hidden-feature alignment. PixelREPA adapts feature alignment to pixel-space clean-image prediction ( Shin et al., 2026 ) . Nevertheless, it retains hidden representations as the alignment target, potentially imposing demands that compete with pixel reconstruction within shared model capacity. This motivates aligning clean-image predictions themselves: our method provides additional supervision for the denoising task without requiring hidden features to match a separate representation target, with conditional consistency and variance reduction established under a Markov coupling for optimal predictions. 3 Motivation and Analysis Preliminaries: x x -prediction.
